title: Delivering New Genes With Engineered Viruses
endLine: Engineered viruses deliver genes into living cells, bounded by size and controls.

scenes.tts: How do you put a chosen gene inside a living cell? A gene alone cannot simply cross a cell membrane. Instead, biologists use engineered viruses, called viral vectors, to carry chosen genes into target cells.
scenes.caption: How do you put a chosen gene inside a living cell? A gene alone cannot simply cross a cell membrane. Instead, biologists use engineered viruses, called viral vectors, to carry chosen genes into target cells.
scenes.visual: One carried world begins: a large schematic living cell fills 65% of frame height, with a glowing solid gene bar outside its intact membrane. As the question plays, the lone gene bar drifts against the membrane and bounces gently back. Then a schematic hexagonal viral shell glides in, encloses the gene bar, and moves toward the cell surface; the label 'Viral vector' appears after it settles. Slow ambient drift keeps the frame moving; use only simple geometric shapes, never molecular structures.

scenes.visual: The schematic cell and approaching viral vector continue slow ambient drift in the background as the title 'Delivering New Genes With Engineered Viruses' fades in large at full contrast and fades out.

scenes.tts: Researchers pack a chosen gene into an engineered virus, such as a retrovirus or an adeno-associated virus. The vector enters the target cell and delivers that gene. The cell then builds the new protein, such as a missing channel or a light-gated channel.
scenes.caption: Researchers pack a chosen gene into an engineered virus, such as a retrovirus or an adeno-associated virus. The vector enters the target cell and delivers that gene. The cell then builds the new protein, such as a missing channel or a light-gated channel.
scenes.visual: Continuing in the same schematic cell world: a coloured gene bar slides into a schematic viral shell (labelled 'Retrovirus', then morphing smoothly to 'AAV'). The shell docks at the membrane, passes inside, and releases the gene bar into the cell interior. From that bar, a simple schematic channel archway builds and glides into the membrane, opening when a soft beam of light touches it ('Light-gated channel').
scenes.narration: Researchers pack a chosen gene into an engineered virus, such as a retrovirus or an adeno-associated virus. The vector enters the target cell and delivers that gene. The cell then builds the new protein, such as a missing channel or a light-gated channel.

scenes.tts: Not every gene fits in one shell. A conventional adeno-associated virus, or A A V, carries about four point seven to five kilobases. A kilobase is a thousand DNA letters. Otoferlin's coding sequence is about six kilobases before a promoter switch is added. So two vectors carry separate parts, and cells receiving both rejoin the full gene.
scenes.caption: Not every gene fits in one shell. A conventional adeno-associated virus, or AAV, carries about 4.7 to 5 kb. A kilobase is a thousand DNA letters. Otoferlin's coding sequence is about 6 kb before a promoter switch is added. So two vectors carry separate parts, and cells receiving both rejoin the full gene.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the schematic AAV shell beside the cell, paired with a computed 0 to 7 kb scale bar (1 kb = 1,000 DNA letters) showing AAV capacity shaded at 4.7 to 5 kb. A computed 6 kb bar labelled 'Otoferlin (6 kb)' slides beside the shell and overflows its slot, with a small schematic 'Promoter' block waiting outside. The bar splits into two schematic parts loaded into two AAV shells (blue and amber); both enter the cell and snap together into one full-length bar.
scenes.narration: Not every gene fits in one shell. A conventional adeno-associated virus, or AAV, carries about 4.7 to 5 kb. A kilobase is a thousand DNA letters. Otoferlin's coding sequence is about 6 kb before a promoter switch is added. So two vectors carry separate parts, and cells receiving both rejoin the full gene.

scenes.tts: Splitting a gene carries a cost. Suppose each of two vectors independently reaches seventy percent of inner hair cells. What fraction of those cells can make full-length otoferlin? Pause and find the overlap.
scenes.caption: Splitting a gene carries a cost. Suppose each of two vectors independently reaches 70% of inner hair cells. What fraction of those cells can make full-length otoferlin? Pause and find the overlap.
scenes.visual: The single schematic cell zooms smoothly out into a 10-by-10 grid of 100 schematic inner hair cells (computed counts). Blue vector particles tint 70 cells (70%); amber vector particles independently tint 70 cells (70%). The question appears large at top: 'Each reaches 70% independently. What fraction makes full-length otoferlin?'
scenes.narration: Splitting a gene carries a cost. Suppose each of two vectors independently reaches 70% of inner hair cells. What fraction of those cells can make full-length otoferlin? Pause and find the overlap.

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen over the 100-cell grid while the 70 blue and 70 amber highlights gently pulse and drift, giving the viewer time to multiply before the overlap resolves.

scenes.tts: Because both deliveries are independent, multiply the two fractions. Zero point seven times zero point seven is zero point four nine, or forty-nine percent. Even at seventy percent per vector, fewer than half the cells build full-length otoferlin. Viral vectors deliver chosen genes into living cells, but size and controls bound every claim.
scenes.caption: Because both deliveries are independent, multiply the two fractions. 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49, or 49%. Even at 70% per vector, fewer than half the cells build full-length otoferlin. Viral vectors deliver chosen genes into living cells, but size and controls bound every claim.
scenes.visual: The 100-cell grid aligns into a computed 10-by-10 area diagram: 7 columns light blue (0.7), 7 rows light amber (0.7), and their 7-by-7 overlap glows bright gold (49 of 100 cells). As each number is spoken, '0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49 (49%)' builds step by step below the grid. The grid then folds back into a single schematic cell as the guiding rule appears briefly.
scenes.narration: Because both deliveries are independent, multiply the two fractions. 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49, or 49%. Even at 70% per vector, fewer than half the cells build full-length otoferlin. Viral vectors deliver chosen genes into living cells, but size and controls bound every claim.

scenes.tts: Getting a gene inside is only half the test. Restoring a lost current, called rescue, still needs vector and expression controls to rule out delivery effects. Even then, rescue cannot tell a channel pore from an overexpressed substitute. And preserving cones in animal models is still not a human trial.

scenes.visual: Back on the single schematic cell: a flat schematic current trace jumps upward when a vector delivers a gene ('Rescue'). Beside it, a matching schematic control cell receives an empty vector with an expression gauge ('Vector & expression controls'). Inside the membrane, a question mark splits between a schematic pore icon and a substitute icon. Then a schematic cone-cell silhouette carries a clear tag: 'Animal models ≠ human trial'.

scenes.tts: With tight controls, viral vectors unlocked three landmark results. In 2006, Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka used retroviruses on mouse connective-tissue cells, called fibroblasts. Delivering twenty-four stem-cell genes, then omitting one at a time, left four gene-switching transcription factors. Those four turned mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells, or i P S cells.
scenes.caption: With tight controls, viral vectors unlocked three landmark results. In 2006, Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka used retroviruses on mouse connective-tissue cells, called fibroblasts. Delivering 24 stem-cell genes, then omitting one at a time, left four gene-switching transcription factors. Those four turned mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells.
scenes.visual: In the same cell world, the schematic cell morphs into a spindle-shaped mouse fibroblast ('2006 · Takahashi & Yamanaka'). Schematic retrovirus shells deliver 24 coloured gene bars; bars drop out one by one until four remain, labelled 'Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc'. The fibroblast smoothly rounds into a glowing schematic stem-cell colony labelled 'iPS cells'.
scenes.narration: With tight controls, viral vectors unlocked three landmark results. scenes.tts: In 2018, Pan and colleagues probed a working channel. A vector delivered altered T M C one into mutant mouse hair cells, restoring current. Each copy carried one added cysteine, an amino acid. A reagent that cannot cross the membrane grabs cysteine where water reaches it. When it altered ion flow in working cells, neither synthesis nor delivery had changed.

scenes.visual: The cell transforms into a schematic mouse hair cell ('2018 · Pan & colleagues', sub-tag 'Tmc1/Tmc2 double-null'). A schematic viral vector delivers a gene bar labelled 'Tmc1 (one added cysteine)', restoring a schematic channel in the membrane and steady current. Outside the membrane, schematic reagent dots reach the exposed site in the water but never cross the membrane; the schematic current trace then shifts while the current is still flowing, crossing out 'Synthesis / delivery'.

scenes.tts: In 2019, Al-Moyed and colleagues worked around the size limit for otoferlin. They split its coding sequence between two A A V two six vectors. Cells receiving both joined the parts back into the full-length gene. From stem cells to hearing channels, engineered viruses answer questions only within cargo and control limits.
scenes.caption: In 2019, Al-Moyed and colleagues worked around the size limit for otoferlin. They split its coding sequence between two AAV2/6 vectors. Cells receiving both joined the parts back into the full-length gene. From stem cells to hearing channels, engineered viruses answer questions only within cargo and control limits.
scenes.visual: Returning to the schematic inner hair cell ('2019 · Al-Moyed & colleagues'): the blue and amber schematic AAV2/6 shells enter together, and their two partial otoferlin bars snap into one glowing full-length gene bar. Three small schematic badges for the three unlocked findings align gently along the bottom as the main cell settles to center.
